content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding Docker Fundamentals: Namespaces and Cgroups"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Docker containers rely heavily on Linux kernel features to provide isolation and resource management. Two of the most critical foundational components are Namespaces and Control Groups (Cgroups). While virtual machines emulate an entire hardware stack, Docker containers share the host kernel while using these two mechanisms to create a secure, sandboxed environment."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"What are Linux Namespaces?"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Namespaces wrap a global system resource in an abstraction that makes it appear to the processes within the namespace that they have their own isolated instance of the global resource. When you run a Docker container, Docker creates a set of namespaces for that container."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"PID (Process ID): Isolates the process ID space, meaning container processes have their own numbering starting from 1."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"NET (Networking): Manages network interfaces, routing tables, and IP addresses independently inside the container."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"MNT (Mount): Provides isolation of the filesystem mount points."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"IPC (Inter-Process Communication): Controls access to shared memory and semaphore segments."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"UTS (UNIX Timesharing System): Allows a single system to appear to have different hostname and domain name."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"USER (User ID): Isolates UID and GID ranges, allowing a user to be root inside a container while being an unprivileged user on the host."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Inspecting Namespaces on the Host"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can inspect the namespaces of running processes on a Linux host using the 'lsns' command. To find namespaces associated with a specific container, you first need to find the process ID (PID) of the container."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' <container_name>"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Once you have the PID, you can list the namespaces associated with that process:"},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"lsns -p <PID>"},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"What are Control Groups (Cgroups)?"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"While namespaces handle what a process can see, Control Groups (Cgroups) handle how much system resources a process can consume. Cgroups limit, account for, and isolate the resource usage of a collection of processes. Without cgroups, a single runaway container could exhaust all CPU and memory on the host machine."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"CPU: Limits CPU shares, quotas, and specifies which CPU cores a container can use."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Memory: Enforces hard and soft limits on RAM usage and swap space."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"I/O: Sets limits on read/write rates for block devices."},{"order":21,"type":"subheading","text":"Limiting Resources with Docker"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Docker provides direct flags to interact with cgroups when launching containers. For instance, you can restrict a container to use a maximum of 512 megabytes of memory and 1.5 CPU cores using the following command:"},{"order":23,"type":"code","text":"docker run -d --name constrained_container --memory='512m' --cpus='1.5' nginx"},{"order":24,"type":"subheading","text":"Verifying Cgroup Limits"},{"order":25,"type":"paragraph","text":"On modern Linux systems using cgroup v2, you can verify these limits directly on the host filesystem. Docker stores container cgroup data in the '/sys/fs/cgroup/docker/' directory. You can check the memory limit of the container by viewing the memory.max file:"},{"order":26,"type":"code","text":"cat /sys/fs/cgroup/docker/<container_long_id>/memory.max"},{"order":27,"type":"heading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":28,"type":"paragraph","text":"Namespaces and Cgroups are the foundational pillars of containerization. Namespaces deliver isolation (security and privacy), while Cgroups deliver resource governance (stability and performance). Understanding these mechanisms demystifies how Docker operates under the hood."}]
